title: Judge a name, price or pack change by mind-share movement, not by product specs
hypothesis: If we judge a name, price or pack change by whether it wins a slot in the shopper's mind, then fewer changes get shipped as pure spec upgrades, because a brand move and a product move need different proof.

signal.check: A proposed name, price or pack change is being scored only on cost or feature specs, with no question about what slot in the shopper's mind it is meant to win.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source gives a number for this judgment habit

risk.note: A review habit, not a shipped change.

steps: Before approving a name, price or pack change, write down the mind-share slot it is meant to win.
Ask if the change is really a product fix, not a brand move, and route it accordingly.
Reject changes judged only on cost or a spec sheet with no stated slot.

test.method: Add the question to the approval checklist for any name, price or pack change.
test.measure: Whether the approval note names a mind-share slot.

title: Cut every PDP or hero message to the one line a scrolling shopper reads in 3 seconds
hypothesis: If we cut the PDP and hero headline to 1 idea with at most 2 supporting bullets, then more mobile shoppers grasp the offer before they scroll away, because the mind holds very few slots per category.

signal.check: The PDP or hero has more than 1 headline idea, or more than 2 supporting bullets, competing for attention.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources give no number, only the rule of 1 idea plus up to 2 to 3 messages

risk.note: Copy edit only; easy to revert.

steps: List every claim in the current PDP hero and headline.
Pick the 1 claim the brand can own and prove.
Cut the rest to at most 2 supporting bullets below the fold.
Read the new hero aloud in 3 seconds to check it lands.

test.method: A/B the trimmed hero against the current one on the top PDP.
test.measure: bounce_rate_pdp and cvr_pdp_to_cart
test.read_point: After 2 weeks or 1,000 sessions per arm, whichever is later

title: Map the category ladder before writing any positioning claim
hypothesis: If we ask real shoppers, or use search and review data as a proxy, which brands come to mind first in our category, then the positioning claim will fit our real rank, because a claim written for the wrong rung reads as false.

signal.check: No one on the team can say, with evidence, whether the store is the first, second, or an unranked name shoppers think of in this category.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the source gives no baseline for how a store's rank changes

risk.note: A research step; no live change until the claim is rewritten.

prerequisites: Customer reviews or on-site search term data
A list of real category alternatives
steps: List every alternative a shopper could pick in this category, including doing nothing.
Ask 10 to 15 real or recent shoppers which brands come to mind first, unprompted.
If interviews are not possible, pull the store's own search terms and review mentions as a proxy and label the ladder a proxy.
Record who ranks first, second, third, and who is missing.
Write down the store's rung and the evidence used to reach it.

test.method: Run 10 to 15 unprompted category-naming interviews, or pull 90 days of search and review data if interviews are not possible.
test.measure: The stated rung and the evidence behind it.
test.read_point: After the interviews are done or after 90 days of proxy data

title: Check who already claims a slot before writing a first or only claim
hypothesis: If we check the category's top marketplace and search results before writing a first or only claim, then fewer claims get made that a rival can disprove in public, because first means first to claim the slot, not first to invent.

signal.check: A draft ad, PDP or press line uses the word first, only, or original with no check of who else already claims that slot.

risk.note: An unproven first claim risks a public correction or a marketplace policy strike.

steps: Search the category's Amazon, Flipkart or Google Shopping results for anyone already using the claim.
If someone already claims the slot, use claim a slot first language instead of second is nowhere language.
Drop or rewrite any claim that cannot survive a public fact check.

test.method: Manual search check before any first or only claim ships.
test.measure: Whether the claim survived the search check unchanged.
test.read_point: Before each new claim is published

title: Avoid repeating the category leader's exact promise on the PDP or a comparison page
hypothesis: If we check the leader's exact promise before writing our own, then we pick an angle they do not already own, because copying their claim invites the question of why we are not the leader.

signal.check: The store's PDP or comparison page makes the same core promise (fastest, cheapest, free shipping) as the recognised category leader.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources give named historical cases, not a general lift figure

risk.note: Copy change only.

prerequisites: A written statement of the category leader's main promise
steps: Write down the leader's exact claim as shown on their own listing or ads.
Compare it to the store's own PDP promise.
If they match, pick a different angle the leader's own listing does not use.

test.method: Manual comparison of the two promises before each new PDP or ad launch.
test.measure: Whether the two promises still match.

title: Check whether the mind will accept the wanted position before spending on it
hypothesis: If we check whether shoppers already have a fixed opinion that blocks the wanted position, then we avoid spending a budget the mind will simply refuse, because a strong product and sales force still fail against a slot the mind will not open.

signal.check: A positioning plan targets a slot (for example premium or first-in-category) with no check of whether shoppers already hold a fixed, contrary opinion of the brand.

risk.note: Skipping this check risks wasted ad spend on a position the market rejects.

prerequisites: Category ladder result from BRD-003
steps: List what shoppers already believe about the brand, from reviews and support tickets.
Check if the wanted position contradicts that belief directly.
If it does, look for a position the brand already owns a related claim to, and build from there instead.

test.method: Compare the wanted claim against a sample of real reviews and support tickets.
test.measure: Whether the claim contradicts an existing, widely held belief about the brand.
test.read_point: Before the positioning statement is finalised

title: Take the against position when a recognised leader already holds the slot
hypothesis: If we state our rank relative to a recognised leader instead of claiming to be better, then the claim reads as credible, because the against position borrows the leader's own frame of reference.
does_not_apply_when: No recognised leader exists in the category yet

signal.check: A recognised category leader exists, and the store's ads make a vague better than everyone claim instead of naming its rank against that leader.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources give named historical cases (Avis, 7-Up), not a general figure

risk.note: Messaging change only.

prerequisites: A named category leader
steps: Name the actual leader in the prospect's mind.
Write the claim as a stated relation to that leader (for example, we are the smaller, faster alternative), not a vague superiority claim.
Check the claim can also read as a what we are not statement for a genuinely new category.

test.method: A/B the against-position headline versus the current vague claim.
test.measure: cvr_overall and ctr on the ad or hero.
test.read_point: After 2 weeks or 1,000 sessions per arm

title: Find an unclaimed creneau dimension instead of fighting the category leader head-on
hypothesis: If we search for an unclaimed dimension (size, price, gender, age, time of day, distribution, or heavy-user framing), then the brand can claim a real open slot, because copying a dimension someone already owns fails.
does_not_apply_when: The brand can already claim the number 1 spot outright

signal.check: No dimension of the category (size, price tier, age group, time of day, channel, or usage frequency) is uniquely claimed by the store yet.

expected_effect.size: unknown; named historical cases only (Volkswagen, Aim, NyQuil, L'eggs)

risk.note: A positioning exercise; nothing ships until a claim is chosen.

prerequisites: Category ladder result from BRD-003
Competitor claim list
steps: List every dimension the category can be cut on: size, price, gender, age, time of day, distribution channel, and usage frequency.
Mark which dimension each competitor already owns.
Pick the open dimension closest to a real product truth.
Draft a claim that owns that one dimension first.

test.method: Review the dimension list with the team and pick 1 open dimension to test in the next positioning statement.
test.measure: Whether an open dimension was found and claimed.

title: Check a new SKU idea for a real mind-gap before treating it as a catalogue-gap fix
hypothesis: If we check whether a proposed new SKU fills a gap shoppers actually notice, not just a gap in the product range, then fewer SKUs launch with no real slot in the buyer's mind, because a factory gap is not a mind gap.

signal.check: A new SKU is proposed mainly because it fills a hole in the internal product range, with no customer request or search demand behind it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; named historical failures only (Edsel, Frost 8/80)

risk.note: A launched SKU that fails still costs cash and shelf or catalogue attention to unwind.

prerequisites: Search term and review data for the proposed SKU category
steps: Write the reason for the new SKU in 1 sentence.
Check if that reason is an internal range gap or a real, voiced customer need.
If it is a range gap only, pause the SKU and look for a reverse extension instead (see BRD-097).

test.method: Search on-site search terms and reviews for demand signals before greenlighting the SKU.
test.measure: Whether a real customer demand signal exists for the SKU.
test.read_point: Before committing to production or MOQ

title: Name the primary shopper in the homepage hero and route everyone else to a secondary collection
hypothesis: If we write the homepage hero for 1 named primary shopper and move gift, wholesale or other buyers to a secondary link, then conversion for the core buyer improves, because a hero written for every buyer dilutes the message for all of them.
does_not_apply_when: The brand already dominates its category and needs no further positioning work

signal.check: The homepage hero tries to speak to gift shoppers, self-purchasers and wholesale buyers all at once, with no single named audience.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources argue the mechanism (sacrifice, smallest viable market), not a lift figure

risk.note: Homepage copy change; easy to revert.

prerequisites: Sales and traffic data by buyer type if available
steps: Identify the single largest or most valuable buyer segment.
Rewrite the hero headline and image to speak only to that segment.
Add a small secondary link or banner for other buyer types (gift, wholesale, etc).
Check reviews are not alienating for stating a clear audience; some pushback is expected and normal.

test.method: A/B the narrowed hero against the current all-buyer hero.
test.measure: cvr_overall for the primary segment and overall bounce rate.
test.read_point: After 2 weeks or 1,000 sessions per arm

title: Size the target market by how many repeat buyers at the store's own AOV and margin sustain the business
hypothesis: If we size the target as the minimum number of repeat buyers the store's own AOV and margin need, then marketing effort concentrates on a real, sustainable segment instead of a vague mass market, because a narrow target served obsessively can outperform a broad one served thinly.

signal.check: No one has calculated how many repeat buyers, at the store's real AOV and margin, are needed to hit the revenue goal.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources give other-brand anecdotes (1,000 true fans, 600 daily seats), not a store-specific number

risk.note: A planning exercise.

prerequisites: AOV, gross margin and revenue goal figures
steps: Divide the revenue goal by AOV times gross margin times expected repeat purchases per buyer per year.
Segment that number by the belief or worldview the buyer holds, not by age or income.
Write the target as a story a buyer tells themselves, not a demographic.

test.method: Recalculate the sizing whenever AOV, margin or the revenue goal changes materially.
test.measure: The stated minimum buyer count and its worldview description.

title: Plot the brand on 2 XY maps against every real shopper alternative, not just direct rivals
hypothesis: If we plot the brand and every real alternative, including doing nothing and out-of-category brands, on 2 different axis pairs, then an overlooked open corner becomes visible, because the crowded middle needs an ad budget the store may not have.

signal.check: No positioning map exists that plots the brand against out-of-category alternatives on axes shoppers actually weigh, like price versus delivery speed.

risk.note: A workshop exercise, not a live change.

prerequisites: Competitor set from a web check
steps: Pick 2 axes shoppers weigh at checkout, from a menu like price, speed, purity, or distribution.
Plot every real alternative, including doing nothing, DIY, and out-of-category brands.
Mark the crowded middle and any open corner.
Re-run with at least 1 different axis pair.
Confirm the brand does not sit on top of competitors on both axes.

test.method: Run the mapping exercise with the team using 2 different axis pairs.
test.measure: Whether an open, defensible corner is found on at least 1 map.

title: Reposition a named competitor with one verifiable fact and a legal review, never a we're better ad
hypothesis: If we name a competitor's specific, verifiable weakness instead of running a we're better ad, then the claim is more persuasive and defensible, because comparative ads invite the question of why we are not the leader.
does_not_apply_when: No open creneau exists and no competitor fact can be verified

signal.check: The brand is considering an ad or page that names a competitor with only a general superiority claim, not a specific verifiable fact.

expected_effect.size: unknown; named historical cases only (Tylenol, Wise, Royal Doulton)

risk.note: Comparative claims about a named competitor carry legal and marketplace-policy risk; verify and clear before shipping.

prerequisites: A specific, verifiable fact about the competitor's product
Legal review in every selling country
steps: Study the competitor's product, not the store's own, for a verifiable weakness (ingredient, policy, slowness).
Write the claim as a specific, checkable statement, never we're better.
Send the claim for legal review of comparative claims in every selling country.
Confirm no competitor mark, logo or product image is used.
Change internal operations first if the claim depends on something not yet true.

test.method: Ship the reviewed claim and track branded search or awareness lift versus the pre-claim baseline.
test.measure: Unaided awareness or branded search share.
test.read_point: 12 to 15 months after launch, per the source's own tracking window

title: Reposition the category around a frustration the leaders all share
hypothesis: If we name a real, voiced frustration the category's leaders all share and build the store's angle around fixing it, then a small-budget brand can compete without outspending the category, because the angle has likely never appeared in the leaders' own ads.
does_not_apply_when: No shared, voiced customer frustration with the category leaders exists

signal.check: Reviews or support tickets show a recurring complaint about the category as a whole, not just about 1 competitor.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 named historical case only (Milk Duds)

risk.note: Messaging change; easy to revert.

prerequisites: Review and support ticket text for the category
steps: Read reviews and support tickets for recurring complaints about the category, not just 1 rival.
Write the complaint as a customer would say it.
Build the store's angle as the alternative that fixes that shared complaint.
Identify the real customer behind the complaint, not an assumed one.

test.method: A/B the new category-reframe headline against the current claim.
test.measure: cvr_overall and click-through on the new angle.
test.read_point: After 2 weeks or 1,000 sessions per arm

title: Anchor a genuinely new product format to something shoppers already know
hypothesis: If we describe a new format as the nearest familiar thing without its downside, then shoppers understand it faster, because the mind resists a genuinely new category unless it is explained against an old one.

signal.check: A genuinely new product format or category is described only with a features list and no comparison to something shoppers already understand.

expected_effect.size: a controlled anchor test raised awareness from 23 percent to 47 percent versus 27 percent to 25 percent for the non-anchored version (Mailgram case)

risk.note: Copy change only.

steps: Identify the nearest familiar product or service to the new format.
Write the headline as the X without the downside of X.
Replace a features-first description with the anchor comparison on the PDP.

test.method: A/B the anchored headline against a plain features list on the PDP.
test.measure: cvr_pdp_to_cart and time on page.
test.read_point: After 2 weeks or 1,000 sessions per arm

title: Check whether the real barrier is the category or the place, not the product, before spending on positioning
hypothesis: If we check whether the real blocker sits one level above the product, such as the category's own reputation, then we avoid wasting positioning spend defending a product that was never the problem.

signal.check: Sales are weak in a way that a product fix has not solved, and the category or the store's home market carries a reputation problem the product cannot fix alone.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 named historical case only (Sabena, Belgium)

risk.note: A diagnostic step.

steps: List the top objections in reviews and lost-sale support tickets.
Check if the objection is about the product, or about the category or place it comes from.
If it is one level up, address the category or place perception before rewriting product claims.

test.method: Tag lost-sale reasons as product-level or category-level for 90 days.
test.measure: Share of lost-sale reasons that are category-level, not product-level.
test.read_point: After 90 days of tagged support and review data

title: Borrow a real, independent authority to justify a premium price or an inconvenience
hypothesis: If we cite a genuine, current third-party list, rating or certification instead of a self-made claim, then a premium price or an inconvenience reads as earned, because a self-made top 10 claim is an invented claim.
does_not_apply_when: No genuine third-party list, rating or certification exists for the brand

signal.check: The store's marketing implies outside recognition (a top list, a rating, a certification) with no real, current third party behind it.

risk.note: A self-made or expired authority claim breaks override 1 and risks a legal or trust problem if challenged.

prerequisites: A verified, current third-party list, rating or certification
steps: List every implied outside authority in current marketing.
Verify each one is real, independent and current with a web check.
Remove any self-made or expired claim.
Cite only verified authorities going forward.

test.method: Audit all current marketing copy for authority claims and verify each one.
test.measure: Number of unverifiable authority claims found and removed.
test.read_point: One-time audit, then on every new claim

title: Replace a category-cliche hero image with one shoppers have not scrolled past before
hypothesis: If we check competitor hero images before shooting a new one, then the store avoids a cliche shot shoppers have already tuned out, because generic category imagery gets scrolled past without registering.

signal.check: The PDP or packaging hero image uses the same setting, angle or prop style as most competitor listings in the category.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources argue the mechanism, not a lift figure

risk.note: A new hero image can be swapped back if it underperforms.

prerequisites: A set of competitor hero images for comparison
steps: Collect the top 10 competitor PDP or ad hero images in the category.
Note the shared visual cliches (angle, setting, prop style).
Brief a hero image that avoids every shared cliche.
Also scan the touchpoint for scam-like signals (flashing elements, robotic pauses) that make shoppers distrust it on sight.

test.method: A/B the new hero image against the current one.
test.measure: ctr and cvr_pdp_to_cart.
test.read_point: After 2 weeks or 1,000 sessions per arm

title: Calibrate creative refreshes to be 1 step ahead of the category, not 10
hypothesis: If we set the creative refresh 1 step ahead of the category's current norm instead of a radical leap, then the brand reads as current without alienating today's buyer, because a brand only needs to be a little ahead of its nearest rival.

signal.check: A planned creative refresh jumps far ahead of what any current competitor is doing, with no current competitor as a reference point.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 named case only (JetBlue vs Virgin America)

risk.note: A creative brief adjustment.

prerequisites: Current competitor creative for reference
steps: Collect the most current creative from 2 or 3 direct competitors.
Set the refresh 1 visible step ahead of that set, not a full reinvention.
Check the refresh still reads as clearly the same brand.

test.method: Show the new and current creative to a small panel unfamiliar with the brand.
test.measure: Whether the new creative reads as current but recognisable, not alien.
test.read_point: Before the creative direction is locked

title: Write the 3-sentence promise and use it in every hero and PDP headline
hypothesis: If we write the promise as a belief, an aspiration and a transformation in 3 sentences, then every headline can be checked against it, because a promise this specific is easy to test for on any page.

signal.check: No written 3-sentence promise exists, and headlines are written from instinct with no shared template to check against.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a template, not a measured threshold

risk.note: A written document; no live change until headlines are rewritten.

prerequisites: Customer language from reviews or support
steps: Fill blank 1 with a belief the customer already holds, not a demographic.
Fill blank 2 with an aspiration the customer already pursues.
Fill blank 3 with a concrete emotional transformation.
Check the homepage hero, top PDP and lead ad each contain at least 1 of the 3 blanks.

test.method: Score the current homepage hero, top PDP and lead ad against the 3-sentence promise.
test.measure: Number of the 3 blanks present on each asset.
test.read_point: After the promise is written and checked against live pages

title: Decide whether the segment runs on affiliation or dominion and write the tone to match
hypothesis: If we check whether the buying moment is about belonging or about winning and write the tone to match, then acquisition creative resonates better, because averaging the two frames speaks to neither.

signal.check: Ad and creative briefs use a generic aspirational tone with no decision on whether the segment buys for belonging or for winning.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source gives the mechanism, not a lift figure

risk.note: A briefing change.

prerequisites: Real customer language from reviews or UGC comments
steps: Read 20 to 30 real customer comments or reviews for language about belonging (we, community, trust) versus winning (I did this, power, achievement).
Decide the dominant frame for the purchase moment being targeted.
Write the ad or influencer brief in that frame only, not averaged with the other.

test.method: A/B an affiliation-framed ad against a dominion-framed ad for the same offer.
test.measure: ctr and hook_rate.
test.read_point: After the ad set reaches at least 10,000 impressions per variant

title: Define us narrowly and explicitly in every people like us statement
hypothesis: If we replace a vague us with a narrow, explicit description in manifestos and About pages, then the statement actually means something to a reader, because a vague us persuades no one.

signal.check: The About page or manifesto uses phrases like people like us or our community with no explicit description of who that is.

risk.note: Copy edit only.

steps: Find every use of us, we, or our community in brand copy.
Replace each vague use with a specific, named description of the shared belief or behaviour.
Check a stranger reading the line would know exactly who it means.

test.method: Manual copy audit of the About page and manifesto.
test.measure: Number of vague us statements replaced with specific ones.

title: Build an exclusive cohort the group controls, not just an elite tier outsiders can revoke
hypothesis: If we design a loyalty tier around belonging the group itself grants, not just a status label the store hands out, then members stay engaged longer, because a group-controlled sense of belonging is harder to lose than an assigned status.

signal.check: The loyalty or VIP tier is defined only by spend thresholds and a badge, with no member-to-member interaction or group-granted status.

risk.note: A loyalty program feature can be rolled back if unused.

prerequisites: An existing loyalty or VIP program, or plans to build one
steps: Add a member-to-member element (referral badges, community shoutouts, peer recognition) to the loyalty tier.
Let members grant or recognise each other's status, not only the store.
Track whether members who receive peer recognition repeat purchase more than those who only hit a spend threshold.

test.method: Compare repeat rate between members who received peer recognition and those who only hit the spend threshold.
test.measure: repeat_rate_365d for each group.
test.read_point: After 6 months of the peer-recognition feature running

title: Run the commodity-swap test: would a switched customer even notice?
hypothesis: If we ask whether a customer switched to the nearest competitor would notice or care, then we get an honest read on whether a real brand exists yet, because a brand that would not be missed is not yet a brand.

signal.check: No one has asked, in a structured way, whether customers would notice or complain if switched to the nearest competitor.

risk.note: A diagnostic question, not a live change.

steps: Ask 10 to 20 recent customers what they would miss if the brand disappeared and a competitor replaced it.
Score the answers for specific, unique reasons versus generic ones.
If most answers are generic, treat brand-building as the priority over performance spend.

test.method: Run the commodity-swap question in a post-purchase survey or support call sample.
test.measure: Share of answers naming a specific, unique reason to stay.

title: Prove a position works in a small test before spending to scale it
hypothesis: If we require a small proof of traction before scaling acquisition spend on a new position, then fewer budgets are wasted on an unproven message, because dominating 1 market or segment first de-risks the next one.

signal.check: A new positioning claim or SKU is about to get scaled ad spend with no small-scale test of who lights up first.

expected_effect.size: a source reports about 8 of 10 new products fail within 3 months in the US, unverified figure

risk.note: A staged spend plan; the small test itself has limited downside.

steps: Pick 1 small market, segment or channel to test the new position or SKU first.
Set a spend cap and a clear signal for success (repeat purchase, not just clicks).
Only scale spend to the next market once traction is confirmed.
Repeat the identical claim in the next market rather than reinventing it.

test.method: Run the position or SKU in 1 limited market or channel before wider rollout.
test.measure: Repeat purchase rate and cvr_overall in the test market.
test.read_point: After the test market reaches a meaningful sample, at least 100 orders

title: Match brand story and channel to the audience's existing worldview, not a new one
hypothesis: If we write creative to affirm a belief the audience already holds instead of trying to change it, then the message lands faster, because changing a belief is far harder than affirming one.

signal.check: A creative brief or channel choice asks the audience to adopt a new belief or identity rather than affirming one they already hold.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources argue the mechanism, not a figure

risk.note: A creative brief change.

prerequisites: Customer language showing existing beliefs
steps: Read customer reviews and support messages for the beliefs customers already hold about the problem the product solves.
Write the creative to affirm that belief, not challenge it.
If a rite or ritual needs replacing, replace the ritual while keeping the same underlying need it served.

test.method: A/B a belief-affirming message against a belief-challenging one for the same offer.
test.measure: ctr and cvr_overall.
test.read_point: After the ad set reaches at least 10,000 impressions per variant

title: Answer the 6 positioning questions in writing before any positioning creative is made
hypothesis: If we write answers to what we own, what we want, whom we outgun, do we have the money, can we hold it, and does execution match, then positioning creative starts from a checked foundation instead of a guess.

signal.check: A positioning or rebrand project is starting creative work with no written answers to the 6 core positioning questions.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a discipline, not a measured lift

risk.note: A written exercise before spend.

prerequisites: Category ladder result
Budget and timeline commitment from the founder
steps: Write 1-line answers to: what position do we own, what position do we want, whom must we outgun, do we have enough money, can we stick it out, does our execution match.
Merge in the simpler 4-question version (why care, what's different, who for, what are we changing) if a lighter pass is needed.
Do not start creative work until all 6 are answered.

test.method: Review the written 6 answers with the founder before approving any creative brief.
test.measure: Whether all 6 questions have a written answer.

title: Test 2 positioning frames against each other before committing budget to either
hypothesis: If we test 2 distinct positioning anchors as 2 ad creatives or 2 landing page heroes before committing, then the store avoids locking in the weaker frame, because a small test reads awareness or click response directionally before a full rollout.

signal.check: A choice between 2 plausible positioning frames is being made by opinion or vote, with no small test run first.

expected_effect.size: a controlled awareness test moved 1 frame from 23 percent to 47 percent while the other frame fell from 27 percent to 25 percent (Mailgram case)

risk.note: A short ad or landing page test.

prerequisites: 2 plausible positioning anchors already in the shopper's mind
steps: Identify at least 2 anchors already familiar to shoppers.
Write 1 distinct theme per anchor, without blending them.
Run each as a separate ad creative or landing page hero.
Read the result as directional, since a click test measures response, not full positioning.
Roll out the winning frame and hold it; retest with the full instrument 12 to 15 months later.

test.method: Split traffic evenly between the 2 framed ads or landing pages.
test.measure: ctr and cvr_overall per frame.
test.read_point: After each arm reaches at least 1,000 sessions or 2 weeks, whichever is later

title: Run the positioning statement checklist before any positioning statement ships
hypothesis: If we run the 15-point positioning statement checklist before shipping a new statement, then common failures (no rung named, 2 or more claims, a too-broad or too-narrow target) get caught before spend, because each row has a known fix.

signal.check: A positioning statement is about to be used in a brief or launched with no structured review against the known failure modes.

risk.note: A review step.

prerequisites: A drafted positioning statement
steps: Check the category is in the customer's own words, not internal taxonomy.
Check the ladder rung is named with evidence, not assumed.
Count the claims; cut to 1.
Check the claim is not head-on with the leader's exact claim.
Check the target is not everyone and not too narrow to sustain the business.
Check every claim word is provable against the brand record.
Check the reading level is below tenth grade.

test.method: Run the checklist against the drafted statement with a second reader.
test.measure: Number of checklist rows passed out of 15.
test.read_point: Before the statement is approved for use

title: Run a full positioning program: ladder, XY map, and the 3-sentence promise
hypothesis: If we run the full positioning program in sequence (category ladder, alternative list, XY map, promise, statement) rather than skipping to a slogan, then the resulting statement is grounded in real evidence and holds up for years.

signal.check: The brand has no written positioning statement, or the current one was written without the ladder, XY map or promise steps.

risk.note: A written document; nothing ships until the founder signs off.

prerequisites: Product facts and provable claims
Customer language
A competitor set
Budget and runway answer from the founder
steps: Write the category the way a customer says it.
Map the ladder from real prospects or a proxy.
List every real alternative, including doing nothing.
Plot 2 XY maps with different axis pairs.
Answer the 6 positioning questions.
Write the 3-sentence promise and the 1-sentence positioning statement.
Check every claim word against the brand record.
Run the positioning statement checklist (see BRD-029).

test.method: Deliver the full positioning statement and map document for founder sign-off.
test.measure: Checklist 5.1 pass rate on the final statement.
test.read_point: At sign-off, then again 12 to 15 months later

title: Run the reposition-the-competition procedure when no open creneau exists
hypothesis: If we follow a fixed sequence to study, verify, and legally clear a competitor-facing claim, then the store gets the persuasive power of naming a real weakness without the legal exposure of an unverified attack.
does_not_apply_when: An open creneau already exists and no leader needs repositioning

signal.check: The team wants to run a comparative or competitor-naming campaign with no structured verification and legal review process in place.

risk.note: Naming a competitor without legal review risks a takedown, a lawsuit, or a marketplace policy strike.

prerequisites: A verifiable, specific competitor fact or a widely shared category frustration
steps: Study the competitor's product for a structural, verifiable weakness.
If no single competitor is the target, name the shared category frustration instead.
Write the claim as a specific, verifiable statement, never we're better.
Change internal operations first so any implied promise is true.
Check the claim creates a resolvable tension, not fear.
Send for legal review of comparative claims in every selling country before shipping.
Track unaided awareness and competitor attribute scores after launch.

test.method: Run the full P3 sequence and track the P2 measurement instrument after launch.
test.measure: Unaided awareness and attribute scores versus the competitor.

title: Decide price as a positioning signal before restructuring price points
hypothesis: If we set price as part of the position, not after it, then price stops contradicting the brand's other claims, because a price point is itself a story the buyer reads.

signal.check: A price change is being decided by cost and margin math alone, with no check against the position the brand claims elsewhere.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources argue the mechanism, not a lift figure

risk.note: A price change is reversible but can shake existing customer trust if reversed often.

prerequisites: Category price band from a web check
steps: Write the brand's current position statement or claim.
Check the proposed price against that claim: does it match a value, mid, or premium story?
Only finalise price once it agrees with the stated position.

test.method: Review any price change proposal against the written position before approval.
test.measure: Whether the price and the stated position agree.

title: Build premium perception through content, story and distribution, not price alone
hypothesis: If we invest in content, partnerships and distribution instead of raising price alone, then the brand can earn a premium perception even at a modest price point, because premium is a function of the whole story, not the number on the tag.

signal.check: The brand wants a premium perception but has invested only in raising the price, with no matching content, partnership or distribution story.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources give named cases (an under $3 can positioned as champagne-tier), not a general figure

risk.note: Content and story investment can be paused if it does not move the needle.

prerequisites: Segment profiles
steps: List the current price point and the perceived tier it sits in.
Pick 1 lever besides price to invest in: content, partnership, or distribution channel.
Build 1 concrete asset in that lever (a story, a collab, a new retail door) and measure perception before and after.

test.method: Survey a small panel on perceived quality tier before and after the new asset ships.
test.measure: Perceived tier score and aov.
test.read_point: 8 to 12 weeks after the new asset launches

title: Price inside the category's learned range unless a valid, first-mover premium story exists
hypothesis: If we keep price inside the category's learned range unless we have a valid, provable story for a new band, then we avoid a price 2 to 3 times the norm that the same shopper generally rejects.
does_not_apply_when: The brand is genuinely first to open a premium band in the category with a valid, provable story

signal.check: The store's price sits well above the category's learned range with no first-mover story or valid reason on record.

expected_effect.size: price 2 to 3 times the category norm generally fails with the same shopper (single operator's practice)

risk.note: Repricing can be reverted but may confuse existing customers if done often.

prerequisites: Category price band from a web check
steps: Pull the category's price range from at least 5 competitor listings.
Compare the store's price to that range.
If well above the range, write the specific, provable story that justifies it, or bring price back inside the range.

test.method: Compare price against the researched category band.
test.measure: Whether the price sits inside the band or has a documented justification for sitting above it.

title: Ask the ten-times question before adding any premium tier
hypothesis: If we ask what would justify charging 10 times more before adding a premium tier, then we reject more-of-the-same tiers that add cost without adding a real story, because more words or a bigger portion do not multiply willingness to pay.

signal.check: A proposed premium tier only adds more quantity, bigger packaging, or extra features, with no new story, scarcity, or relationship angle.

risk.note: A planning question before launch.

steps: Write what the premium tier adds beyond quantity or features.
Ask if that addition is a different story, scarcity, curation, or relationship, not just more of the same.
Reject the tier if the answer is only more of the same.

test.method: Review the tier proposal against the ten-times question before greenlighting.
test.measure: Whether the tier passes with a real story answer.

title: Stop using price cuts to build trust on high-ticket or premium items
hypothesis: If we stop cutting price to reassure hesitant high-ticket buyers, then the premium position holds, because lowering price on a considered purchase can read as a lack of confidence rather than reassurance.
does_not_apply_when: The store's position is value-led and discounting is part of its normal story

signal.check: Cart abandonment on high-ticket items is being addressed mainly with discount codes rather than proof, reviews near the price, or financing options.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source's own illustration cites repeated 40 to 60 percent off as damaging, not a general threshold

risk.note: Removing a discount is reversible, but test the effect before a full rollback.

steps: List the current discount tactics used on high-ticket items.
Replace 1 discount touchpoint with proof: reviews near the price, financing or pay-later messaging, or a guarantee.
Track cart-to-checkout conversion with and without the discount.

test.method: A/B a proof-led cart page against the discount-led version for the same high-ticket item.
test.measure: cvr_cart_to_checkout.
test.read_point: After 2 weeks or 500 sessions per arm

title: Reframe exclusivity as an unused narrative angle, not a stockout
hypothesis: If we build exclusivity as a story competitors have not used, instead of leaning on out-of-stock messaging, then the premium position holds without an operations failure being mistaken for marketing.
does_not_apply_when: A drop or seasonal-withdrawal model with true, temporary scarcity is the actual business model

signal.check: Marketing copy uses selling fast or limited stock language on a daily-use or replenishment product, when the real cause is a demand-planning gap.

risk.note: A fabricated or misapplied scarcity claim risks trust and a marketplace policy strike.

prerequisites: Real stock data to confirm whether scarcity is true
steps: Classify the product as a drop-style limited item or a daily-use replenishment item.
For daily-use items, remove stockout-as-marketing language and fix demand planning instead.
For drop-style items, write an exclusivity narrative angle competitors have not used, backed by a provable product fact.
Never fabricate a stock counter; match any low-stock badge to the real stock file.

test.method: Audit current urgency and scarcity copy against real stock data.
test.measure: Number of scarcity claims that do not match the real stock file.
test.read_point: One-time audit, then on every new urgency claim

title: Map what exclusive means per segment and awareness stage before writing premium copy
hypothesis: If we map what exclusivity means to each real segment and awareness stage, then premium copy speaks to what that specific buyer actually values, because 1 assumed exclusivity trigger rarely fits every buyer.

signal.check: Premium copy uses 1 assumed exclusivity trigger for all buyers, with no split between unaware and comparing shoppers or between segments.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source gives no method, only the requirement

risk.note: A research and copy exercise.

prerequisites: Segment profiles from avatar research
steps: List the store's known buyer segments.
For each segment, note what triggers a sense of exclusivity for them specifically.
Split unaware shoppers from those already comparing options.
Write 1 aspirational identity line per segment.

test.method: Run segment-specific premium copy against the current 1-size-fits-all version.
test.measure: cvr_overall by segment.
test.read_point: After 2 weeks or 1,000 sessions per segment

title: Write a marketing vector and ad-variance spectrum before running premium acquisition
hypothesis: If we write a core positioning vector and the spectrum of ad concepts allowed, then media buyers can run varied, aggressive ads without drifting off the premium position.

signal.check: Media buyers and creators have no written vector or spectrum document, so premium ad concepts vary by whoever made the last one.

risk.note: A written document, easy to revise.

prerequisites: A finalised positioning statement
steps: Write the core positioning, identity mirrored, and story told in 1 page.
Write the spectrum of ad concepts and angles allowed, from safest to most aggressive.
Write the promotional intensity rule in advance (maximum discount depth and share of days on promotion).
Share the document with every media buyer and creator before briefs go out.

test.method: Score new ad concepts against the vector document before launch.
test.measure: Share of new ad concepts that pass the vector check on first review.
test.read_point: After the first month of using the document

title: Test whether the premium lifestyle image still signals the brand's promise with the product removed
hypothesis: If we check that a lifestyle hero image still communicates the brand's promise with the product edited out, then the creative sells an aspiration, not just a product photo, because premium buyers often buy the ability to be seen, not only the item.

signal.check: The premium hero image or ad is generic lifestyle stock with no buyer-specific aspiration attached, and would say nothing about the brand with the product removed.

expected_effect.size: unknown; opinion-based sources, no measured figure

risk.note: A creative review step.

steps: Take the current premium hero image and mentally or digitally remove the product.
Ask if the image still signals the brand's specific promise and audience.
If it reads as a generic lifestyle shot with no aspiration, rebrief the creative with a named buyer aspiration.

test.method: Show the product-removed image to a small panel and ask what brand or promise it implies.
test.measure: Whether panel answers match the intended brand promise.
test.read_point: Before the creative direction is locked

title: Cast real practitioners and community members, not stock models, in premium lifestyle video
hypothesis: If we cast real practitioners and community members instead of paid models in premium video, then recall and trust improve, because sexual or supermodel-level beauty imagery can suppress brand recall.

signal.check: Premium video creative uses only paid stock models with no real practitioners, customers, or founder appearances.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources argue the mechanism, and 1 study reports lower recall for extreme-beauty and sexual creative versus real-people creative

risk.note: A casting choice for the next creative batch.

prerequisites: Access to real practitioners, customers, or community members willing to appear on camera
steps: Identify 3 to 5 real practitioners, customers, or community members willing to be filmed.
Brief a 15 to 30 second lifestyle mini-documentary format, not a scripted ad.
If founder-led, include a founder documentary segment.
Compare hook and hold rate against the current stock-model creative.

test.method: A/B the real-practitioner video against the current stock-model creative.
test.measure: hook_rate and hold_rate.
test.read_point: After the ad set reaches at least 10,000 impressions per variant

title: Track hook rate, hold rate, CTR and cohort retention for premium creative, not ROAS alone
hypothesis: If we track hook rate, hold rate, CTR and cohort retention alongside ROAS for premium concepts, then a slow-building brand ad is not killed early on a ROAS-only read, because equity metrics catch a concept's real effect that short-term ROAS misses.

signal.check: Premium or brand-building ad concepts are being judged and killed on ROAS alone, with no hook rate, hold rate, or cohort retention tracked.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no target values given in the source

risk.note: A reporting change.

prerequisites: Baseline hook rate, hold rate and cohort retention data
steps: Add hook rate, hold rate, CTR and cohort retention to the premium creative dashboard.
Define which movements in these metrics trigger a real iteration, not ROAS alone.
Hold premium concepts to this fuller scorecard before killing them.

test.method: Report the full scorecard for every premium ad concept for 1 full quarter.
test.measure: hook_rate, hold_rate, ctr, cohort retention.
test.read_point: End of the quarter, then quarterly after

title: Change only 1 to 2 percent of a known product format when entering an established category
hypothesis: If we keep the product format close to what the category already knows and spend the saved effort on liquid, design or positioning, then the launch avoids the cost and risk of teaching a new format, because reinventing the container in an established category adds unneeded friction.

signal.check: A new product in an established category is reinventing the container or format instead of matching the category norm.

risk.note: Format and tooling changes are costly to reverse once manufactured.

prerequisites: Category format research
steps: Identify the standard format (size, container, packaging type) the category already uses.
Keep that format and change only 1 to 2 percent of it (a colour, a callout, a material detail).
Redirect saved development budget into liquid, design, or positioning.

test.method: Compare development cost and time to market for a familiar-format launch versus a reinvented one.
test.measure: Development cost and time to market.

title: Design packaging for the channel it must win in and iterate on real sell-through
hypothesis: If we design packaging for the specific channel it must win in and revise it against real sell-through, not internal taste, then packaging failures at shelf or thumbnail size get caught and fixed early.

signal.check: Packaging was designed and approved on a screen or in a design review with no test at the actual shelf or thumbnail distance it will be seen at.

expected_effect.size: 1 self-reported case claims a redesign tripled sales on the same liquid across 2 doors, unverified

risk.note: Packaging redesigns can be iterated but cost tooling and inventory to change.

prerequisites: Access to the real retail shelf or thumbnail view
steps: Identify the decisive channel the pack must win in (shelf, thumbnail, or unboxing).
View the current pack at that real distance or size (2 metres for shelf, 150px for thumbnail).
Add colour coding or callouts in the space the store controls, roughly 65 percent of a regulated pack.
Iterate based on real sell-through, not internal taste, and expect to redesign more than once.

test.method: Compare sell-through of the redesigned pack against the old one in the same channel.
test.measure: units_per_order or sell-through rate.

title: Keep some brand content free to spread and some content or perks worth paying for
hypothesis: If we give away ideas that spread for free and reserve real rewards for paying customers, then the brand still funds itself while keeping word of mouth alive, because giving away everything forfeits the cash flow needed to reinvest.

signal.check: Every piece of brand content, perk, or exclusive is free, with no paid tier or purchase-gated benefit at all.

risk.note: A content and perks policy, easy to adjust.

steps: List current free content, perks, and giveaways.
Identify 1 or 2 that could become a paid or purchase-gated benefit without losing shareability.
Keep the widely shareable ideas free and move the higher-value souvenirs behind a purchase.

test.method: Track sign-ups or purchases before and after 1 perk moves behind a paywall or purchase gate.
test.measure: gross_margin and repeat_rate_365d.

title: Branch PDP and cart layout by AOV band: trust badges for low AOV, proof and financing for high AOV
hypothesis: If we give low-AOV impulse items trust badges and fast checkout, and high-AOV considered items reviews near the price plus financing messaging, then each buyer sees the proof they actually need to convert.

signal.check: The same PDP and cart layout is used for both low-AOV impulse items and high-AOV considered items, with no AOV-specific proof shown.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source covers the low-AOV half of this branch

risk.note: A template change; can be reverted.

prerequisites: AOV by product or category
steps: Split the catalogue into low-AOV and high-AOV bands.
For low-AOV impulse items, add trust badges and simplify checkout steps.
For high-AOV considered items, add reviews near the price, financing or pay-later messaging, and proof before the buy button.
Verify each band's layout against real brand data before rollout.

test.method: A/B the AOV-specific layout against the current 1-size-fits-all layout, split by band.
test.measure: cvr_pdp_to_cart and cvr_checkout_to_order per band.
test.read_point: After 2 weeks or 1,000 sessions per band

title: Run the premium signal audit each quarter against the vector and promo intensity rule
hypothesis: If we run the premium signal audit every quarter, then discount creep, sellout misuse, and off-vector creative get caught before they erode the premium position.

signal.check: No structured premium audit has run in the last quarter, and no one has checked promo cadence, sellout handling or creative cast against the written vector.

risk.note: An audit process.

prerequisites: A written marketing vector and promo intensity rule
6 to 12 months of promo calendar data
steps: Check the triad (exclusivity narrative, aspirational identity, lifestyle story) appears across the PDP, home, and top ad.
Check price sits inside the band or has a valid above-band story.
Review the last 6 to 12 months of the promo calendar against the intensity rule.
Check sellout handling matches the product type (drop vs daily-use).
Check the creative scorecard tracks hook rate, hold rate, CTR and cohort retention next to ROAS.
Check refund, breach and delay behaviour matches the premium promise.

test.method: Run the full checklist 5.6 each quarter and log pass and fail rows.
test.measure: Number of checklist rows passed out of 12.

title: Run the full premium positioning program before launching a premium tier or brand
hypothesis: If we run the full premium positioning sequence (segment mapping, exclusivity angle, price-band decision, vector, creative format, measurement) in order, then a premium launch holds together instead of shipping mismatched pieces.

signal.check: A premium product or tier is being launched with pieces built independently: pricing decided separately from creative, with no shared vector document.

risk.note: A launch plan; individual pieces can still be adjusted before spend commits.

prerequisites: Product quality that holds up on first use
Segment profiles
Promo history
Category price band
steps: Map psychology per segment: what each values, aspires to, and what triggers exclusivity for them.
Choose the exclusivity angle: a provable, unused narrative, never a stockout.
Decide the price band and answer the ten-times question for any premium tier.
If pricing inside the band, spend the saved difference on product, design and positioning.
Write the marketing vector and the spectrum of ad variance.
Brief 15 to 30 second lifestyle mini-documentaries with real practitioners.
Instrument hook rate, hold rate, CTR and cohort retention next to ROAS.
Run the premium signal audit each quarter.

test.method: Track the full premium scorecard from launch through the first 2 quarters.
test.measure: aov, hook_rate, hold_rate, cohort retention.
test.read_point: End of quarter 1 and quarter 2 post-launch

title: Write brand strategy in a document before any visual design work starts
hypothesis: If we write purpose, values and the brand strategy down before opening a design tool, then approval meetings judge against the written strategy instead of becoming a taste fight, because a written framework stops that drift.

signal.check: A rebrand or new identity project has moodboards or logo concepts already in progress with no written strategy document to check them against.

risk.note: A process change, not a live asset.

steps: Stop any in-progress visual design work.
Write purpose, mission, vision and 3 to 5 values in 1 page.
Get founder sign-off on the written strategy before visuals resume.

test.method: Check for a signed-off strategy document before the next design review.
test.measure: Whether the document exists and is dated before the first visual concept.

title: Build brand strategy from 4 inputs: vision, business strategy, values and customer understanding
hypothesis: If we build the central brand idea from vision, business strategy, values and customer understanding together, then the strategy holds for employees and partners, not only for buyers, because a strategy missing 1 of the 4 usually breaks somewhere later.

signal.check: The current brand strategy statement was written from only 1 or 2 of the 4 inputs (for example, only customer research, with no link to business strategy or team values).

risk.note: A workshop exercise.

prerequisites: Business goals in writing
steps: Run 4 separate brainstorms: values and beliefs, features and benefits, voice and tone, look and feel.
Group each brainstorm into clusters and note what resonates most.
Write 1 unifying idea that connects vision, business strategy, values and customer understanding.
Check the idea would make sense to an employee or partner, not only a buyer.

test.method: Review the unifying idea with 1 employee and 1 partner outside the marketing team.
test.measure: Whether both can restate the idea in their own words.

title: Fix 3 to 5 non-negotiable core values and use them to filter every approval
hypothesis: If we fix 3 to 5 non-negotiable values and check every mood board, asset or partnership proposal against them, then approvals stop being a taste debate, because a value that can reject a real proposal is doing real work.

signal.check: Approval meetings for creative, partnerships or sign-off decisions have no written values to check proposals against.

risk.note: A decision-making habit.

steps: Write 3 to 5 values as short, testable statements.
For each value, write 1 example of a real proposal it would reject.
If a value cannot reject anything, rewrite it or drop it.
Use the values as the first filter in every mood board, sketch, or partnership review.

test.method: Track how many proposals get rejected on a values check over the next quarter.
test.measure: Number of proposals rejected citing a specific value.

title: Turn discovery findings into a few how-might-we challenges as a later decision test
hypothesis: If we convert repeated discovery themes into a small number of written how-might-we challenges, then later creative and product decisions have a clear acceptance test, because a vague theme cannot be checked against a design choice.

signal.check: Discovery research (interviews, reviews, support tickets) produced repeated themes that were never converted into a written decision test.

risk.note: A written exercise.

prerequisites: Discovery research with repeated themes
steps: List the themes that repeated across interviews, reviews or support tickets.
Write 2 to 3 how-might-we challenges from the strongest themes.
Use each challenge as an acceptance test for later creative or product decisions.

test.method: Check whether a sample of recent decisions can be traced back to a how-might-we challenge.
test.measure: Share of recent major decisions with a traceable challenge.

title: Show differentiation in imagery and copy customers grasp in seconds, do not just declare it
hypothesis: If we demonstrate the difference visually and in copy instead of declaring it, then a stranger can infer the position from the page alone, because the ideal ad is simple enough to be the strategy statement.

signal.check: The PDP or hero copy states the brand is different or better with adjectives, but no image or specific proof actually shows the difference.

risk.note: A creative brief change.

steps: List every place the copy declares the brand is different without proof.
Replace each declaration with a specific image, comparison, or demonstration.
Show the revised page to someone unfamiliar with the brand and ask what makes it different.

test.method: 5-second test: show the revised hero to an unfamiliar person for 5 seconds and ask what the brand stands for.
test.measure: Whether they name the intended difference unprompted.

title: Change operations first so every brand claim on the page is actually true
hypothesis: If we fix the underlying operation before publishing a claim about it, then the claim survives scrutiny and builds trust instead of breaking it, because behaviour must match the image, not the reverse.

signal.check: A claim on packaging, a listing, or a page (fast shipping, easy returns, always in stock) does not match what actually happens operationally.

risk.note: Operational fixes can take longer than a copy change, but leaving a false claim live risks trust and refund disputes.

prerequisites: A claims register listing every current on-page claim
steps: List every operational claim currently made on packaging, listings or pages.
Check each claim against real fulfilment, support, and return data.
Fix the operation first, or remove the claim if it cannot be fixed soon.

test.method: Audit claims against operational data quarterly.
test.measure: Number of claims not matching real operations.

title: Write the founder or brand story as Self, Us, Now
hypothesis: If we write the founder story as Self (who we are), Us (why this audience should care), and Now (a concrete call to act), then About pages and launch emails move a reader to act, because this structure gives a reason to care and a next step, not just a biography.

signal.check: The About page or founder video is a straight biography with no clear Us section (why this audience specifically) or Now section (a concrete call to act).

risk.note: A copy rewrite.

steps: Write the Self section: who the founder is and what they did, without exaggeration or fake vulnerability.
Write the Us section: why this specific audience should care.
Write the Now section: a concrete, peer-backed call to act.
Rewrite the About page or founder video script in this order.

test.method: A/B the restructured About page against the current version.
test.measure: Time on page and email sign-up or follow rate from the page.

title: Create tension, never fear, in acquisition and cart-recovery copy
hypothesis: If we write urgency as a resolvable pull instead of a scare, then acquisition and cart recovery copy converts without eroding trust, because fear paralyses while tension resolves with 1 simple action.

signal.check: Cart-recovery emails, launch scarcity, or acquisition copy use scare language or fabricated deadlines instead of a real, resolvable pull.

risk.note: Fabricated urgency risks trust and platform policy issues; check the deadline is real before shipping.

steps: Review current cart-recovery and launch copy for fear language or fake deadlines.
Rewrite each as a real, resolvable pull (a genuine restock date, a real limited batch).
Confirm every urgency claim is true before it ships.

test.method: A/B the tension-based copy against the current fear-based copy.
test.measure: cvr_cart_to_checkout and unsubscribe rate.
test.read_point: After 2 weeks or 500 sends per arm

title: Name the enemy as a belief or category habit, never a person, and clear any competitor fact with legal review
hypothesis: If we frame the brand's enemy as a belief or category habit instead of a named person or an unreviewed competitor claim, then the manifesto builds identity without legal or reputational risk, because naming a person invites backlash that a belief does not.

signal.check: A brand manifesto, ad, or About page names a specific person or an unreviewed competitor claim as the enemy.

risk.note: Naming a person or an unverified competitor claim risks legal and reputational blowback.

steps: Find every place the brand names a person or an unreviewed competitor claim as an enemy.
Rewrite as a belief, category habit, or a verified, legally reviewed competitor fact.
Check the rewritten line disagrees with an institution or habit, not a person.

test.method: Audit current manifesto and ad copy for enemy framing.
test.measure: Number of person-named or unreviewed enemy claims found and fixed.

title: Say who a price or policy change is for and who it is not for
hypothesis: If we state clearly who benefits and who loses when a price or policy changes, then existing customers get an honest frame instead of silence, because naming the trade-off directly turns some resistance into a story fairness-minded customers can support.

signal.check: A price increase or policy change (loyalty terms, shipping fees, subscription tiers) is being announced with no explanation of who it helps and who it costs.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 named case only, prices up about 20 percent with no tipping

risk.note: A price or policy change itself may not be reversible without further customer confusion; the communication approach is low risk.

steps: Write who gains from the change and why.
Write who loses something and name it honestly.
Communicate both sides in the announcement instead of hiding the trade-off.

test.method: Send the honest-framing announcement and track churn or complaint volume against a past change made without this framing.
test.measure: subscription_churn and support ticket volume after the announcement.

title: Design packaging and unboxing so the customer has a specific reason to tell a friend
hypothesis: If we design an unboxing or post-purchase moment around 2 questions (what will I tell my friends, why will I tell them), then the product spreads by visible use, because private-use products do not get talked about on their own.

signal.check: The unboxing or post-purchase experience has no obvious, shareable moment, and the product is used privately with no visible cue.

expected_effect.size: 1 cited anecdote reports a Wii unboxing video viewed about 71,000 times in a week

risk.note: A packaging or unboxing addition, easy to test.

steps: Ask what a customer would tell a friend after unboxing, in their own words.
Check the benefit to the friend, not just the brand, is clear in that sentence.
Add 1 visible, shareable element to the unboxing (a card, an insert, a visible design detail) that makes the product visible in use.

test.method: Track UGC mentions or referral link use before and after the unboxing change.
test.measure: other:referral_share_rate.

title: Build a referral incentive with real tension and a status story, not just a discount code
hypothesis: If we give a referral program a real incentive plus a status or belonging story, then more customers actually refer, because a referral link with no incentive, tension, or status story gets ignored.

signal.check: The referral program offers only a generic discount code with no status element, urgency, or story attached to sharing it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the fix names a known failure case (HugDug) with no incentive or story, not a lift figure

risk.note: A program design change; can be reverted.

prerequisites: An existing or planned referral program
steps: Review the current referral incentive for a real reason to act (not just a discount).
Add a status element: an early-access perk, a named tier, or public recognition for top referrers.
Add a resolvable urgency (a real limited window), never a fabricated one.
Relaunch the program and compare referral rate to the old flat-discount version.

test.method: A/B the redesigned referral incentive against the current flat-discount version.
test.measure: other:referral_share_rate.

title: Reframe the customer journey as tension and relief steps, not a features dump
hypothesis: If we design onboarding and PDP flow as a sequence of tension and relief instead of a flat features list, then customers stay engaged through the journey, because showing the result before the method builds pull.

signal.check: Onboarding emails or the PDP content sequence read as a flat list of features with no built-in tension or payoff structure.

risk.note: A content sequencing change.

steps: Map the current onboarding or PDP content as a flat list.
Show the end result or transformation first, not the method.
Sequence remaining content as a series of small tensions each resolved by the next step.

test.method: A/B the resequenced onboarding flow against the current flat-list version.
test.measure: email_click_rate and completion rate through the flow.

title: Copy a proven business or launch model and spend original effort on story and experience
hypothesis: If we reuse an already-proven business or launch structure instead of inventing a new one, then scarce original effort goes into story and experience, because a proven structure removes 1 major source of launch risk.

signal.check: A new launch or business model is being built from scratch with no check of whether a proven structure already exists to copy.

risk.note: A planning choice.

steps: List 2 or 3 proven business or launch models in adjacent categories.
Pick the closest fit and copy its structure rather than inventing a new one.
Spend the saved effort on the story and experience layer instead.

test.method: Compare time to launch for a copied-structure plan versus an original-structure plan.
test.measure: Time to launch and launch-week readiness.

title: Separate goal, strategy and tactics, and hold the strategy for years
hypothesis: If we write the goal, the strategy and the tactics as 3 separate layers and only change tactics year to year, then the brand avoids abandoning a working position out of internal boredom.

signal.check: Annual planning changes the core strategy every year, or the team cannot separate goal, strategy and tactics in the current plan.

expected_effect.size: unknown; named cases of 30-plus year strategy stability (Patagonia), not a general figure

risk.note: A planning framework change.

steps: Write the goal (the outcome wanted), the strategy (the basic position held) and the tactics (this year's execution) as 3 separate lines.
In the next planning cycle, change only the tactics line unless a real market shift forces the strategy to change.
Check any proposed strategy change against R141's accountant rule before approving it.

test.method: Review the last 2 annual plans and check whether strategy or only tactics changed.
test.measure: Whether the core strategy line stayed the same year over year.

title: Write a subscription brand's promise around the replenishment ritual, and name tiers clearly
hypothesis: If we write the brand promise around the replenishment ritual instead of only the first purchase, and name tiers so a shopper can say which one they are in, then subscribers feel located in the brand's structure, which supports retention.

signal.check: The brand's promise and homepage copy speak only to the first purchase moment, with no mention of the replenishment ritual, and tiers have no clear, sayable names.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source for the promise-writing part, flagged as general practice in the source playbook

risk.note: A copy and naming change.

steps: Write 1 sentence describing the replenishment ritual (when, how, and why the customer reorders).
Add that ritual to the brand promise, not just the first-purchase story.
Name each subscription tier so a shopper can say out loud which tier they are in.
Add churn-aware messaging (a check-in, a pause option) tied to the ritual, not only a win-back discount.

test.method: A/B the ritual-aware promise and tier names against the current first-purchase-only copy.
test.measure: subscription_churn and repeat_rate_90d.

title: Run the full brand strategy workshop to produce a written brand brief
hypothesis: If we run the full workshop sequence (goals, 4 questions, 4 brainstorms, values, purpose, promise, worldview, tension, enemy, how-might-we, story) in order, then the resulting brand brief covers every element a later creative or hiring decision needs to check against.

signal.check: No single written brand brief exists that covers purpose, values, promise, worldview, tension and enemy together.

risk.note: A written document.

prerequisites: Business goals in writing
Research from reviews, support tickets, or customer interviews
A facilitator or a structured written exercise
steps: Write the top-line business goals.
Answer the 4 strategy questions: why care, what's different, who for, what are we changing.
Run the 4 brainstorms and fix 3 to 5 values.
Write purpose, mission, vision, the 3-sentence promise and the big idea in under 6 words.
Write the worldview, the tension, and the enemy as a belief or habit, never a person.
Write 3 how-might-we challenges and the Story of Self, Us, Now.
Check every sentence against the brand record and the reading level rule.

test.method: Score the finished brief against the 9 or 10 brand ideals with a second reader.
test.measure: Ideals score and completeness against the checklist.

title: Replace a placeholder brand name before it becomes permanent
hypothesis: If we replace a rushed placeholder name early instead of letting it stick, then the brand avoids years of compounding friction, because the name appears on every ad, pack, PDP title and subject line.

signal.check: The current brand name was chosen quickly under legal or launch pressure and was never meant to be permanent.

risk.note: A rename after the placeholder has been live for a while carries real switching cost; weigh against R84's rename triggers.

steps: Confirm the current name was a placeholder, not a deliberate choice.
Run the naming project (BRD-078) to find a real replacement.
Decide the rename timing using the rename decision idea (BRD-089) before committing.

test.method: Track how often the placeholder name causes confusion in support tickets or search.
test.measure: other:name_is_placeholder resolved or not.
test.read_point: Before the next major marketing push

title: Run a category, product and buyer audit before generating any name candidate
hypothesis: If we audit the category's naming patterns, the product's real differences, and why buyers buy before generating names, then candidates start from real facts instead of guesswork.

signal.check: Name candidates are being generated with no written list of category naming patterns, product facts, or the buyer's own words for the benefit.

risk.note: A research step.

prerequisites: Customer review and support ticket text
steps: List every name in the category and note the shared pattern.
Write what is actually, factually different about the product.
Write why buyers buy and the ultimate benefit, in the buyer's own words.
Answer 4 questions: how do we define winning, what do we have to win, what do we need to win, what do we need to say.

test.method: Review the completed audit with the naming team before generation begins.
test.measure: Whether all 4 audit elements are documented.

title: Name the brand's ultimate benefit, not the category, and keep the category word in metadata
hypothesis: If a brand-level name captures the ultimate benefit instead of the category word, and the category word still lives in secondary copy and metadata, then the name differentiates without losing search discovery.
does_not_apply_when: Naming a product or collection title, where a descriptive title is the default (see R60)

signal.check: The brand name is purely descriptive of the category (a mop brand called ProMop) with no benefit word and no plan for keeping the category word visible elsewhere.

expected_effect.size: unknown; named cases only (Swiffer, Impossible Burger)

risk.note: A brand name change is a major, low-reversibility decision.

prerequisites: Naming audit (BRD-067)
steps: Identify the ultimate benefit up the ladder from the buyer audit.
Draft brand name candidates around that benefit or a surprising idea, not the category word.
Plan where the category word will live: subtitle, tags, and metadata.

test.method: Check search visibility for the category term after the benefit-led name launches.
test.measure: organic_clicks for category-relevant search terms.

title: Default product and collection titles to descriptive, benefit-first titles for search
hypothesis: If product and collection titles lead with a descriptive benefit visible in the first 60 characters, then search and mobile results convert better, because a coined name at the product level adds no search meaning.

signal.check: Product or collection titles use a coined or abstract name with the benefit or category word missing from the first 60 characters.

expected_effect.size: unknown; named cases only (Spray 'n Wash, Head & Shoulders, DieHard)

risk.note: A title change; reversible.

steps: List current product and collection titles that lead with a coined name.
Rewrite each so the benefit or descriptor appears in the first 60 characters.
Keep the coined brand name only at the parent level.

test.method: A/B the descriptive titles against the current coined titles for a sample of SKUs.
test.measure: organic_clicks and cvr_pdp_to_cart.

title: Screen every naming candidate on the 7 core qualities before it advances
hypothesis: If we screen every name candidate against meaningful, distinctive, future-oriented, modular, protectable, market-positive and visual criteria, then weak candidates get cut before legal or design spend.

signal.check: Name candidates are being shortlisted by gut feel with no structured screen against the 7 core qualities.

risk.note: A screening step.

prerequisites: A list of name candidates
steps: Score each candidate 1 to 5 on meaningful, distinctive, future-oriented, modular, protectable, positive in every market, and visual.
Add the 3 extra jobs: gets attention, holds attention through processing fluency, is surprising.
Drop any candidate scoring poorly on more than 2 criteria.

test.method: Run the scoring sheet with 2 or more reviewers per candidate.
test.measure: Score spread and number of candidates cut.

title: Generate name candidates across all 6 naming types on purpose
hypothesis: If we deliberately generate candidates across founder, descriptive, fabricated, metaphor, acronym and magic-spell types, then the shortlist covers real options instead of 1 team's default style.

signal.check: All current name candidates cluster around 1 or 2 naming types, with no deliberate coverage of the other types.

risk.note: A generation exercise.

prerequisites: Naming audit (BRD-067)
steps: Brief generation separately for each of the 6 types: founder, descriptive, fabricated, metaphor, acronym, magic spell.
Mine roots, mythology, and a cross-category small-things archive for fabricated and metaphor types.
Check the budget and category fit before weighting any 1 type more heavily (small budget leans descriptive or metaphor).

test.method: Count candidates generated per type before moving to the shortlist step.
test.measure: Number of types represented with at least 5 candidates each.

title: Generate far more name candidates than feels necessary before judging any of them
