expected_effect.size: unknown; a small commissioned study (20 subjects, 9-point scale), treat as a panel read, not a finding

risk.note: A small panel test before a packaging or media commitment.

prerequisites: The candidate sensory element and the current visual
steps: Present the visual alone to a small panel and record pleasantness.
Present the sensory element alone and record pleasantness.
Present them together, plus a deliberately mismatched pairing, and record both.
Adopt only a congruent pairing that scores above either element alone.

test.method: Run the 4-step panel test with at least 10 to 20 people.
test.measure: Pleasantness score for visual alone, element alone, congruent pair, and mismatched pair.

title: Test packaging weight and touch for a quality signal independent of function
hypothesis: If packaging weight and touch are tested for perceived quality independent of the actual product function, then a premium claim can be backed by a felt cue, not just a visual one.

signal.check: Packaging weight and material feel have never been tested for perceived quality against the store's premium claim.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 cited case (a lighter remote judged broken by 100 consumers)

risk.note: A packaging test, reversible before a full production run.

steps: Test 2 packaging weight or material options with a small consumer panel.
Ask panel members to rate perceived quality for each option, without other context.
Choose the option that best matches the store's stated premium claim.

test.method: Run a blind touch test with 10 or more consumers comparing 2 packaging options.
test.measure: Perceived quality score per option.

title: Test brand recall by creative variant before using a sexual or shock hook
lever: sexual or shock creative recall test
hypothesis: If any sexual or shock ad hook is tested for brand recall by variant before scaling, then the store avoids a hook that drives attention but suppresses recall of the brand itself.

signal.check: An ad or PDP image uses sexual or shock content to drive attention, with no test of whether viewers actually remember the brand afterward.

expected_effect.size: 1 cited eye-tracking study of 400 subjects reports recall falling to 9.8 percent versus about 20 percent for men, and 10.85 percent versus 22.3 percent for women, with sexual or shock creative

risk.note: Sexual or shock creative carries reputational and platform-policy risk beyond the recall question.

steps: Identify any current or proposed creative using sexual or shock content.
Test brand recall (not just clicks) for that creative against a non-sexual, non-shock variant.
Drop the sexual or shock variant if it underperforms on recall, even if it wins on clicks.

test.method: Survey exposed viewers on brand recall for both variants.
test.measure: other:brand_recall_score per variant.
test.read_point: After the ad set reaches sufficient reach for a recall survey, typically 10,000-plus impressions per variant

title: Check any co-brand or sponsorship placement for narrative fit before running it
hypothesis: If a sponsorship or co-brand placement is checked for whether the brand is load-bearing in the story, not passive wallpaper, then the placement lifts recall instead of being suppressed by a stronger co-brand or an unwanted association.

signal.check: A sponsorship, collab, or shared-media placement is planned with no check of whether the brand plays a real, load-bearing role in the story, or what association appearing there teaches.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 cited case study (an American Idol screen-time study) with about 400 subjects

risk.note: A weak or unwanted association from a placement can be hard to undo once public.

steps: Ask whether the brand is genuinely load-bearing in the sponsorship or placement's story, not just a background logo.
Ask what association appearing next to this partner or content teaches the audience.
Apply a brand-fit veto regardless of the deal's reach or ROI if the association is wrong.

test.method: Review the placement brief against the narrative-fit and association questions before signing.
test.measure: Whether both questions have a clear, positive answer.
test.read_point: Before the sponsorship or placement is confirmed

title: Keep every low-stock or urgency badge tied to the real stock file, never fabricated
hypothesis: If every low-stock or selling-fast badge is generated from the real stock file, then the store avoids the trust and marketplace-policy risk of a fabricated urgency counter.

signal.check: A low-stock, selling-fast, or limited-quantity badge appears on the PDP with no link to the real, current stock file.

risk.note: A fabricated stock counter breaks the no-invented-claims rule and risks a marketplace policy strike.

prerequisites: Real-time or regularly updated stock data
steps: Audit every urgency or low-stock badge currently shown on the site.
Connect each badge to the real, current stock file, not a static or manually set message.
Remove any badge that cannot be tied to real stock data.

test.method: Spot-check live badges against the actual stock count.
test.measure: Number of badges matching real stock data.
test.read_point: One-time audit, then on every new badge

title: Run the 5 steps of marketing in order instead of skipping straight to spreading the word
hypothesis: If the team runs invent, narrow, tell, spread, and persist in order instead of jumping straight to promotion, then acquisition efforts rest on a real product story instead of pushing a message with nothing behind it.

signal.check: The team is focused on step 4 (spreading the word through ads and content) with no clear step 1 through 3 (a real story, a narrow served audience, a matching narrative) done first.

risk.note: A planning check.

steps: Write what is worth making and the story worth telling about it.
Name the few people it particularly benefits.
Write the story to match their existing narrative.
Only after steps 1 to 3, design the conditions for those people to tell others.
Commit to showing up regularly and generously for years, not a single campaign.

test.method: Review the current marketing plan against the 5 steps and flag any skipped.
test.measure: Number of steps completed before spend increases.

title: Build products and messages from the market's own lock, not an internal change story
hypothesis: If the roadmap and positioning start from a real customer lock instead of a grandiose internal change story, then resources go to a fit the market actually wants, because reverse-engineering a story to justify what is already made wastes effort.

signal.check: A new product or campaign is being justified with an internal change narrative that was written after the product was already decided, not from a real customer need.

risk.note: A planning discipline.

prerequisites: Customer language from reviews or support
steps: Write the real customer lock (the specific need or frustration) before writing the product or campaign story.
Check whether the current plan was reverse-engineered from an existing product to justify it.
Reject a grandiose, unresourceable change story in favour of a lock the team can actually address.

test.method: Review the next 3 product or campaign briefs for a documented customer lock.
test.measure: Share of briefs with a real customer lock documented before the solution.

title: Own a permission asset instead of relying only on platform reach
hypothesis: If the brand builds a real owned permission asset (email, SMS, community), then it is not entirely dependent on rented platform reach, because a platform audience can disappear with an algorithm change.

signal.check: Most audience reach comes from platform followers or ad reach, with no growing, engaged email or SMS list of its own.

risk.note: A channel investment, easy to adjust.

steps: Add a clear, low-friction email or SMS capture point to every high-traffic touchpoint.
Move engaged social followers toward the owned list with a real incentive.
Test whether people would notice or ask where the brand went if it stopped posting; that is the real permission test.

test.method: Track list growth rate and engagement before and after adding capture points.
test.measure: list_size and flow_revenue_share.

title: Judge organic content by revenue and owned-audience growth, not views or followers
hypothesis: If organic content is judged by revenue and owned-audience growth instead of views or follower count, then the team stops chasing vanity reach that does not convert.

signal.check: Content success is reported and celebrated using views or follower counts, with no revenue or list-growth metric attached.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 named example of 40 million views generating about 200 dollars of sales

risk.note: A reporting change.

steps: Replace views and follower count as the headline metric in content reports.
Add revenue attributed and owned-list growth per content piece.
Review the last quarter's top content by the new metric, not the old one.

test.method: Re-rank the last quarter's content by revenue and list growth instead of views.
test.measure: Correlation between view rank and revenue rank.

title: Set the give-and-ask rule per brand: soft asks in organic, hard CTAs in paid
hypothesis: If organic content defaults to a soft ask (a mention, a link in bio) while hard CTAs live in paid ads, then organic reach is protected while paid still drives direct conversion, unless the store's one-touch purchase path makes a lighter organic CTA the better fit.
does_not_apply_when: The store's purchase path is one-touch and light organic CTAs cost real, measurable sales

signal.check: Every organic post carries a hard sales CTA with no distinction from paid ad messaging, or the reverse: no path to purchase exists anywhere in organic content.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a documented rule, not a general lift figure

risk.note: A content policy, easy to adjust.

steps: Write the default rule: no hard CTA in organic, ask in paid, link in bio.
Check whether the store's one-touch purchase path is an exception that needs a lighter organic CTA.
Record the choice and track paid performance before and after organic ramps to judge it.

test.method: Compare paid performance before and after organic volume increases under the chosen rule.
test.measure: Paid conversion rate and organic engagement.
test.read_point: After 60 days of the rule being applied

title: Give the founder an early-face role with 1 to 3 content themes and a planned handover point
hypothesis: If the founder appears as the early face of the brand with only 1 to 3 content themes and a planned handover point, then founder-led content builds trust without becoming an unmanageable or unbounded commitment.
does_not_apply_when: The founder has decided to remain the permanent public face indefinitely, which is also a valid choice

signal.check: Founder content is unfocused across many themes with no tracked link to customer acquisition, and no discussion of a future handover point exists.

risk.note: A content focus decision.

steps: Pick 1 to 3 themes the founder will consistently cover.
Track which customers arrive via founder content specifically.
Decide and document either a handover date or the decision to stay the face indefinitely.
Apply the same guideline discipline to the founder's personal brand as to the company brand.

test.method: Tag new customers by whether they arrived via founder content.
test.measure: other:founder_attributed_customers as a share of total.

title: Document the brand's day-one journey on video as a marketing and negotiating asset
hypothesis: If the founder documents the brand's early journey on simple video from day one, then the store builds a content archive that later becomes both marketing material and negotiating currency with partners who lack production capability.

signal.check: No video or photo archive of the brand's early journey exists, and the founder has not started casual, regular documentation.

risk.note: A habit, not a live change.

steps: Start recording short, casual video clips of key moments (production, first sale, first setback) using just a phone.
Store the clips in an organised, dated archive.
Reuse archive footage later in founder story content and partner pitches.

test.method: Check the archive folder for content monthly.
test.measure: Number of clips added per month.

title: Pick 1 platform and 1 content format and go all in
hypothesis: If the team commits to 1 platform and 1 content format instead of spreading thin across many, then content quality and consistency improve, because dabbling across platforms rarely builds real traction on any of them.

signal.check: Content effort is spread thin across 3 or more platforms and formats with no single platform getting sustained, consistent focus.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 2 single-operator opinions agree, not a controlled test

risk.note: A focus decision.

prerequisites: A defined buyer segment
steps: Pick the 1 platform and 1 format the team can sustain consistently, based on fit with the buyer, not follower count.
Publish 3 to 4 niche pieces per 1 broader piece, adjusting the ratio based on view-to-buyer data.
Pause effort on other platforms until this 1 shows traction.

test.method: Compare engagement and conversion from the focused platform against the prior spread-thin approach.
test.measure: Engagement and conversion rate on the focused platform.

title: Identify and over-invest in the customers who already advocate for the brand
hypothesis: If the store identifies its existing superusers and over-invests attention in them, then advocacy compounds, because fixed resources mean not every customer can get the same treatment.

signal.check: No process exists to identify which customers already advocate for the brand (repeat reviewers, frequent UGC posters, referral sources), and all customers get the same generic treatment.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 named case (a daily creator for a year became a major driver and was hired)

risk.note: A segmentation and outreach effort.

prerequisites: Review, UGC, and referral data
steps: Identify the top 20 to 50 customers by reviews, UGC posts, or referrals.
Reach out with a specific, meaningful gesture (early access, recognition, a direct relationship).
Track whether their advocacy increases after the extra attention.

test.method: Compare advocacy activity (reviews, UGC, referrals) for the identified superusers before and after outreach.
test.measure: other:referral_share_rate for the superuser group.

title: Seed a launch through a few respected insiders in a high-trust community
hypothesis: If a launch is seeded through a small number of respected insiders in a high-trust community instead of broad advertising alone, then the message spreads through an existing trust network rather than starting from zero.

signal.check: A new launch relies only on paid ads or broad announcements, with no seeding through a small number of trusted community figures first.

expected_effect.size: unknown; illustrative headcounts only (about 3 at TED, about 15 in a theatre), not a formula

risk.note: An outreach effort.

prerequisites: Identified high-trust communities relevant to the product
steps: Identify 1 high-trust community relevant to the product (a running club, a hobbyist forum, a local group).
Find 3 to 5 respected insiders within that community.
Seed the launch with them first, before or alongside broader promotion.

test.method: Track whether the seeded community shows early adoption before wider promotion starts.
test.measure: Early sales or sign-ups attributable to the seeded community.
test.read_point: In the first 2 weeks after seeding

title: Limit the founder's daily focus to a short priority list and say no to most requests
hypothesis: If the founder keeps a short daily task list and declines most incoming requests, then scarce founder time goes to brand-moving work instead of being consumed by low-value asks.

signal.check: The founder's day is filled reactively with requests and small tasks, with no short, deliberate daily priority list.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a threshold table cites 3 tasks a day and saying no to about 97 percent of requests with no card or measured result behind it

risk.note: A time-management habit.

steps: Write no more than 3 priority tasks each morning.
Default to declining requests that do not serve those 3 tasks.
Review at the end of the week how much time went to the priority list versus reactive requests.

test.method: Track daily task completion against the 3-item list for 2 weeks.
test.measure: Share of days the 3 priority tasks were completed.

title: Run the full audience-building and content system for the brand
hypothesis: If the audience-building system runs as a full sequence (remarkable test, platform choice, give-and-ask rule, calendar, capture, founder plan, permission, revenue judging, persistence) instead of ad hoc posting, then organic content compounds into a real owned audience.

signal.check: Organic content posting happens with no documented system covering platform choice, the give-and-ask rule, a content calendar ratio, or a permission-channel goal.

risk.note: A system build; individual pieces (BRD-149 to BRD-159) can be adopted independently.

prerequisites: A chosen platform and format
The voice sheet
A permission channel
steps: Run the remarkable test: write the sentence a customer would say to a friend, or design an artifact that gives one.
Pick 1 platform and 1 sustainable format.
Set the give-and-ask rule and record the choice.
Set the 3-to-4 niche-to-broad calendar ratio, adjusted on data.
Set up 1 low-friction capture tool for content ideas.
Write the founder content plan with 1 to 3 themes.
Move every engaged viewer toward email or SMS.
Judge the system by revenue and owned-audience growth, and hold it for years unless a real signal says otherwise.

test.method: Track list_size and content-attributed revenue monthly against the pre-system baseline.
test.measure: list_size and other:content_revenue_attributed.

title: Hold the basic brand strategy for years; change the creative only when results say so
hypothesis: If creative is refreshed only when a real signal (the accountant, a measured decline) says so, not when the internal team is bored, then a working position is not abandoned too early.

signal.check: A creative refresh, tagline retirement, or channel cut is being proposed mainly because the internal team is tired of it, with no data showing it has stopped working.

expected_effect.size: unknown; named historical cases of abandoning a working position too early (Mailgram's late switch to next-day delivery)

risk.note: A decision discipline.

steps: Before any creative refresh, check performance data for a real, measured decline.
If no decline exists, treat internal boredom as insufficient reason to change.
Reserve full strategy changes for a failed test, a legal problem, or the runway running out (see BRD-166).

test.method: Review the last 3 creative refresh decisions for whether they were data-driven or boredom-driven.
test.measure: Share of refreshes backed by a real performance signal.

title: Treat consistency, not personal authenticity, as the customer-facing promise
hypothesis: If the brand delivers the same promised experience regardless of a bad day or a founder's mood, then customers get what they were promised every time, because consistency is the professional standard, while chasing constant personal authenticity can break the promise.

signal.check: Customer-facing tone or service quality shifts noticeably with the founder's or team's mood or energy on a given day.

risk.note: A standards discussion, not a live change.

prerequisites: Voice sheet or default voice (BRD-118)
steps: Document the promised tone and service standard regardless of internal mood.
Check recent customer-facing content or support interactions for consistency against that standard.
Address any drift as a training or workflow issue, not as a call for more authenticity.

test.method: Sample support interactions or posts across different weeks for tone consistency.
test.measure: Consistency score across samples.

title: Classify every ad line as performance or brand, and stop killing brand creative on ROAS alone
hypothesis: If every ad line is classified as performance (judged on ROAS, CAC) or brand (judged on branded search lift, repeat rate), then brand-building creative is not killed early for lacking a short-term ROAS it was never meant to deliver.

signal.check: All ad spend, including clearly brand-building creative, is being judged on ROAS or CAC alone, with no separate brand-lift metric tracked.

risk.note: A reporting and budget classification change.

steps: Tag every current ad line as performance or brand.
For performance lines, keep judging on ROAS and CAC.
For brand lines, set branded search lift and repeat rate as the judging metric instead, and do not kill them on ROAS alone.

test.method: Review ad spend allocation and kill decisions against the classification for 1 quarter.
test.measure: Number of brand-tagged lines killed on ROAS alone (should trend to zero).

title: Track position movement with the same instrument over time
hypothesis: If unaided awareness, attribute scores, category association, and the reorder curve are tracked with the same instrument over time, then real position movement becomes visible, instead of guessing from anecdote.

signal.check: No repeatable tracking instrument exists for unaided awareness, attribute scores, or category association, so position movement after a positioning or naming program cannot be measured.

expected_effect.size: 1 named case moved from last to first on 2 attributes in 15 months; another case's unaided awareness almost tripled in about a year

risk.note: A measurement build.

prerequisites: A research budget or a proxy (search terms, review mentions)
steps: Set the baseline: unaided awareness, per-attribute scores, correct category association, and the reorder curve, using a proxy if a research budget is not available.
Re-run the identical instrument 12 to 15 months later for a repositioning, or 90 to 120 days after a name launch.
Report movement, not just the current snapshot.

test.method: Repeat the same tracking instrument at the scheduled interval.
test.measure: Change in awareness, attribute scores, and category association versus baseline.
test.read_point: 12 to 15 months after a repositioning, or 90 to 120 days after a name launch

title: Confirm the funnel and lifetime value are visible before buying ads to build a position
hypothesis: If the store can see lifetime value and the funnel clearly before increasing acquisition spend on a new position, then budget is not committed blind to a funnel that cannot support it.

signal.check: Acquisition spend is being increased to support a new brand position with no clear, current view of lifetime value or the conversion funnel.

risk.note: A pre-spend check.

prerequisites: LTV and funnel reporting
steps: Pull current lifetime value and funnel conversion data before approving new acquisition spend for a position.
If the funnel cannot be seen clearly, fix reporting first (hand to the measurement domain) before committing spend.
Set the acquisition budget only once the funnel and LTV are visible.

test.method: Review LTV and funnel reporting readiness before each new acquisition budget increase.
test.measure: Whether LTV and funnel data were available and reviewed before the spend decision.

title: Overspend in 1 market or channel first, confirm the position lands, then repeat it identically
hypothesis: If a limited budget concentrates on 1 market, segment, or channel first instead of spreading thin everywhere, then the position has a real chance to land somewhere before the identical claim repeats elsewhere.

signal.check: A limited acquisition or positioning budget is being spread evenly across many markets, segments, or channels at once, with no market confirmed as established yet.

expected_effect.size: unknown; named historical rollout cases only (geographic, demographic, chronologic, distribution)

risk.note: A budget allocation change, easy to adjust.

steps: Choose 1 rollout axis: geographic, demographic, a single cohort, or 1 distribution channel first.
Overspend in that 1 area rather than underspending broadly.
Confirm the position is established there (branded search share, repeat purchase) before adding the next market.
Repeat the identical claim in the next market rather than reinventing the message.
Schedule the next markets or channels on a calendar.

test.method: Track branded search share and repeat purchase in the first market before expanding budget to the next.
test.measure: Branded search share and repeat rate in the pilot market.
test.read_point: Before the next market or channel receives budget

title: Bring in a second person to challenge every major positioning or identity decision
hypothesis: If a second person or outside facilitator challenges every major positioning or identity decision, then the design lead's assumptions get tested before launch, because positioning is a game best played by two.
does_not_apply_when: The founder is working entirely alone with no access to a second reviewer of any kind

signal.check: Positioning or identity decisions are being made and approved by 1 person alone, with no outside challenge before launch.

risk.note: A process addition.

steps: Identify 1 person, inside or outside the team, who can act as a genuine challenger.
Share the draft positioning or identity decision with them before finalising it.
If truly working solo, substitute a structured written exercise (writing the counter-argument yourself) and expect less challenge than a real second person provides.

test.method: Track whether every major positioning or identity decision has documented outside input before launch.
test.measure: Share of decisions with a second reviewer's input recorded.

title: Check for real resources and stamina before starting a demanding brand initiative
hypothesis: If the team checks for real resources and stamina before starting a demanding rebrand or launch, then it either commits fully or quits early at the low-commitment point, rather than stalling mid-project.

signal.check: A demanding brand initiative (a rebrand, a major relaunch) is starting with no honest check of whether the team has the resources and stamina to get through its hardest stretch.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this is not every setback, only under-resourced or unprepared projects

risk.note: A pre-commitment check.

steps: Write the hardest stretch the initiative will require (budget gap, time, emotional toll).
Honestly assess whether the team has the resources and stamina for that stretch.
If not, quit at this early, low-commitment point rather than starting and stalling mid-project.

test.method: Review the readiness check with the founder before the initiative kicks off.
test.measure: Whether the check was documented before starting.

title: Separate decision quality from outcome when reviewing a positioning or naming bet
hypothesis: If retros judge whether the positioning or naming decision was reasoned well given what was known, not just whether it happened to work out, then the team learns the right lesson instead of over- or under-crediting luck.

signal.check: A retro on a positioning or naming decision judges it only by the outcome (it worked or it didn't), with no separate assessment of whether the decision process itself was sound.

risk.note: A retro process change.

steps: In the retro, separately score the decision process (was it well-reasoned given known information) and the outcome (did it work).
Note cases where a good decision had a bad outcome, or a bad decision got lucky.
Carry forward lessons about the process, not just about the outcome.

test.method: Run the 2-part scoring in the next 3 positioning or naming retros.
test.measure: Number of retros using the 2-part scoring.

title: Plan for an adoption chasm between early fans and the mass market
hypothesis: If the team plans for a real chasm between early adopters and the mass market, and identifies a genuine network effect or status ratchet as the bridge, then scaling from a niche community to a mass audience is approached realistically instead of assumed to happen from hype alone.

signal.check: A plan to scale from a strong niche community to a mass audience has no identified real bridge (a network effect, a status ratchet) beyond hoped-for word of mouth or hype.

expected_effect.size: unknown; scaling from niche to mass is described as genuinely hard and rarely done

risk.note: A planning exercise; the underlying scaling attempt itself carries real cost and risk.

steps: Name the store's current early-adopter base honestly.
Identify a real network effect or status ratchet that could carry the message beyond that base, not just hoped-for virality.
If no real bridge exists, plan to grow the niche further rather than assuming a jump to mass market.

test.method: Review the identified bridge mechanism with the team before committing to a mass-market scaling plan.
test.measure: Whether a specific, real bridge mechanism is documented.

title: Let taste-led originality happen only in the creative direction step, after customer research
hypothesis: If customer research and the ladder shape the brief first, and personal taste is only used to originate the creative direction and naming tension-zone candidates, then the brand gets both a researched foundation and distinctive creative, instead of picking 1 approach and dropping the other.

signal.check: The team is either skipping customer research entirely in favour of pure founder taste, or letting research and consensus dictate every creative choice with no room for a distinctive, taste-led direction.

risk.note: A sequencing rule for how the team works, not a live change.

prerequisites: Category ladder and customer language research (BRD-003)
steps: Complete the positioning and brand strategy research (ladder, customer language, worldview) before any creative direction work starts.
Once the strategy is set, allow taste-led, distinctive options into the 3-direction creative exploration (BRD-110) and the naming tension zone (BRD-073).
Test the resulting creative in market rather than defending it on taste alone.

test.method: Check that research was completed and documented before the creative direction brief was written.
test.measure: Whether research preceded creative work in the project timeline.

title: Treat a hit-driven, mass-reach plan as a named, budgeted exception, not the default
hypothesis: If a plan to chase a broad hit instead of a narrow, sustainable audience is named explicitly with its own playbook and budget, then the store does not drift into a mass-reach strategy by default without deciding to take on its higher risk.
does_not_apply_when: The store has deliberately chosen and budgeted for a hit-seeking strategy with founder sign-off

signal.check: Marketing plans assume broad, viral-style reach as the default growth path, with no explicit decision or budget set aside for that higher-risk approach versus the default smallest viable market strategy.

risk.note: A strategy classification exercise; the underlying hit-seeking spend itself carries real risk.

steps: Check whether the current growth plan assumes a smallest viable market or a broad hit.
If a hit-driven approach is intended, write it down explicitly with its own budget and get founder sign-off.
Default back to the smallest viable market approach (BRD-011) if no such explicit decision exists.

test.method: Review the current growth plan for an explicit strategy type declaration.
test.measure: Whether the plan states smallest-viable-market or hit-seeking, with budget attached if the latter.
